chapter.title: Compound Components
chapter.description: Components that work together and share state implicitly.

blocks.text: A compound component is a family of components that only make sense together: `Tabs` with `TabList`, `Tab` and `TabPanel`. The parent holds the state and shares it with its children through context.

blocks.caption: The caller controls the markup; the parent controls the behaviour.

blocks.text: The user of the component decides layout, wrappers and ordering, while the shared state stays hidden. This is how most headless UI libraries are built.
Before context was convenient, compound components injected props by cloning their children. You still meet this in older code.

`cloneElement` only reaches direct children, so wrapping a `Tab` in a `<div>` silently breaks it. Context has no such limitation, which is why it is the modern choice. `cloneElement` is now discouraged in the React docs.

previous.title: Composition First
previous.description: The pattern that removes the need for most of the others.

blocks.text: Before reaching for a named pattern, remember that React's core idea already solves most reuse problems: components accept other components.
Give a component named holes for content and let callers fill them. It stays flexible without growing a wall of boolean props.
A specific component is often just a general one with some props filled in. No inheritance required.
React has no component inheritance and does not need it. Wrap and compose instead - it is easier to read and impossible to get into a fragile base class problem.

next.description: The two pre-hooks reuse patterns, why they faded, and where they still fit.

blocks.text: Before hooks, sharing stateful logic meant sharing components. Two patterns dominated, and you will still meet both in existing codebases and libraries.
A component holds the logic and calls a function prop to decide what to render.
A HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new one with extra props or behaviour.

items: **Wrapper hell** - several HOCs nest components deep enough to make DevTools unreadable.
**Prop collisions** - two HOCs that both inject `data` silently overwrite each other.
**Indirection** - it is not obvious from a component where an injected prop came from.
A custom hook has none of these problems: no extra components, no injected props, and the source is visible at the call site.
Wrapping a component in an error boundary or a provider, where you genuinely want an extra component.
Library integrations that must work with class components.

blocks.text: If you write a HOC, copy the display name - `WithUser.displayName = 'withUser(' + Component.displayName + ')'` - or DevTools will show a tree full of anonymous wrappers.
